The three spliced passages in the report ([p.13], [p.14], [p.16]) are there at those page labels; the only differences are whitespace normalisation around punctuation/stress marks and an added closing quote on 'fly'. new_statements.rule_in_words: For Unua (sister dialect of Pangkumu/Rerep): word stress is described as penultimate (on disyllables equivalently initial), including on nouns carrying the fossilised *na article and on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic verb roots; with monosyllabic verb roots the subject/mood prefix does not take stress, so stress stays on the (final) root syllable. Pearce hedges that penultimate placement in longer words may partly be a list-reading effect, and records a set of polysyllables with initial stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p.15: misinov, rroborum and 'other multi-syllable words' noted with initial rather than penultimate stress; p.16: prefix + monosyllabic verb root = stress on the root (word-final) syllable. Morton 1891 for Pangkumu itself adds two lexical remarks: 1sg verb forms in mue'/bue' carry the accent on mue'; ferambur 'busy (hand-full)' accented on a (penult) vs ferambur 'broken hand' accented on e.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, elicited/citation forms; Pearce explicitly raises the possibility that the pattern reflects list reading/reciting intonation. Statement is for Unua (unua1237), not the Pangkumu/Rerep variety; only ~200-character Google snippets of pp. 13-16 were readable, so the opening sentence of the stress section was not seen in full.
new_statements.identity_note: The only description of Rerep/Pangkumu proper is Morton 1891 (Pangkumu village variety, with notes on a northern 'R.' dialect from Rukumbo), which gives no general accent rule. The stress statement quoted is for Unua (Glottolog unua1237, ISO onu), which Lynch & Crowley 2001 (sec. 3.7.13) and Pearce 2015 treat as a dialect of a single Unua-Pangkumu language together with Rerep (rere1240, ISO pgk); Glottolog 5.x keeps them as separate languages under an 'Unua' node. Any catalog entry built from Pearce 2015 should be keyed to unua1237, or to rere1240 only with an explicit sister-dialect flag.

sources.citation: Morton, Alexander. 1891. Grammar of the language spoken at Pangkumu, Malekula. In D. MacDonald (ed.), South Sea Languages, vol. II: Tangoan-Santo, Malo, Malekula, Epi (Baki and Bierian), Tanna, and Futuna, 34-72. Melbourne: Melbourne Public Library / Edgerton and Moore.
sources.note: The 'Alphabet' and 'Letter changes' sections (pp. 34-36) give no general accent rule. Only two item-specific remarks: p. 41 'There are some verbs whose 1st singular is mwe' or mue'.. and the accent is always on the mue''; p. 69 ferambur 'his hand is full/busy' has 'Accent on a' but ferambur 'broken hand' has 'accent on e'. The general 'accent is generally on the penultimate vowel' passage on p. 74 belongs to the following Baki (Epi) grammar, not Pangkumu.
